--- title: "Three time axes" jupyter: coi-docs --- Every measure carries two notions of "when" in its columns, and the release you attached is a third. Conflating them is the characteristic error in this domain. | Axis | Column(s) | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | **Period** | `period_start`, `period_end` | the time the estimate *describes* | | **Source release** | `source_release` | the upstream edition that *published* it | | **Cancer Basemap release** | the folder you attach (`v2026-11-02/`, or `latest/`) | which monthly bundle you are reading | ## A real example: PLACES 2024 vs. 2025 ::: {#bd1a31b4 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
source_release period_start period_end value
0 2024 2022 2022 6.5
1 2025 2023 2023 6.6
``` ::: ::: Two rows, same measure, same county (Denver County, CO). The **source release** is `'2024'` or `'2025'` — the PLACES edition. The **period** each release actually describes is one year *earlier*: the 2024 release models 2022 BRFSS data, the 2025 release models 2023 data. A query that filters on `source_release = '2025'` expecting "2025 data" is filtering on the release label, not the period — the value it gets describes 2023. Both source releases are in every Cancer Basemap release, because `source_release` is a column, not a folder. The **Cancer Basemap release** is the third axis: a bundle holds the current rows only, so if a source corrects a value within one `source_release`, the corrected row replaces the old one in the next bundle. The earlier value stays in the earlier release, which is why a dated folder, or its Hugging Face tag, is how you reproduce an analysis (see [Versions and citation](/guides/versions-and-citation.qmd)). ## A second example: an edition's own period moves SVI's `source_release` **is** the edition, and each edition's own period is a five-year ACS window that moves with it — never the edition year alone: ::: {#e1917e29 .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
edition period_start period_end
0 2000 2000 2000
1 2010 2006 2010
2 2014 2010 2014
3 2016 2012 2016
4 2018 2014 2018
5 2020 2016 2020
6 2022 2018 2022
``` ::: ::: The 2020 edition's period is `2016`–`2020`, not `'2020'` alone — treating an edition's release year as its period would be off by up to four years. ## Why this matters for a catchment report The sentence a cancer center has to defend — *"in our catchment, as reported by source S in release R, the measure was X"* — names the release, not the period, on purpose: the release is what you can point back to when someone asks "where did this number come from." Reproducing a past analysis means filtering on `source_release`, not on `period_start`/`period_end` (a later release can restate an earlier period with revised numbers), and pinning the Cancer Basemap release you attached, since a bundle's rows can change between releases.
